title: What is a rudraksha mala and why do people wear it
description: A plain guide to the rudraksha mala: where the bead comes from, how a japa mala differs from a chain necklace, and why people traditionally wear one.
intro: A rudraksha mala is a string of dried rudraksha seeds, traditionally 108 beads plus one extra guru bead, used for chanting and worn as a sign of devotion to Lord Shiva. People wear it for many reasons: faith, a family custom, a vow during a festival, or simply because the earthy look of the beads feels personal. Here is what the mala actually is, where the tradition comes from, and what to check before you buy one.

sections.heading: Where the rudraksha bead comes from
paragraphs: Rudraksha beads are the dried seeds of a tree from the Elaeocarpus family that grows in the Himalayan foothills, parts of North East India and South East Asia. When the fruit ripens, its blue outer skin is removed and the hard, wrinkled seed inside is cleaned and dried. The natural lines that run from one end of the seed to the other are called mukhis, or faces. When people talk about a five mukhi or a seven mukhi bead, they are counting these lines.

The name joins two Sanskrit words: Rudra, a name of Shiva, and aksha, usually translated as eye or tear. A widely told story says the first rudraksha trees grew where Shiva's tears fell after a long meditation. That is why the bead is so closely tied to Shaiva devotion, and why many people reach for it during Shravan or on Mahashivratri.

sections.heading: What turns beads into a mala
paragraphs: Strictly speaking, a mala is a counting tool for japa, the repeated chanting of a mantra or a name of God. The traditional count is 108 beads, with an extra bead called the sumeru or guru bead that marks the start and end of each round. The beads are usually strung on cotton or silk thread, often red, with a small knot between each one so they do not grind against each other.

Smaller versions are common too. A 54-bead or 27-bead mala is easier to carry, and a wrist mala lets people keep one on them through the day. Some families skip the full string altogether and tie a single bead on a red or black thread, worn at the neck or on the wrist.

sections.heading: Why people choose to wear one
paragraphs: Ask five people why they wear rudraksha and you will probably hear five different answers. The most common ones are:
list: Devotion: it is a visible, everyday way of remembering Shiva, especially for people who follow Shaiva traditions.
Chanting: some keep the same mala for daily japa and wear it between sessions so it stays close.
Family custom: in many homes a mala is given at a thread ceremony, or handed down by a grandparent.
Festivals and vows: Shravan month, Mahashivratri and pilgrimages like the Kanwar Yatra are times many people start wearing one.
Personal style: the brown, textured beads look natural with kurtas and plain tees alike, and plenty of people simply like how they look.

sections.heading: A japa mala and a rudraksha chain are not the same thing
paragraphs: This is where first-time buyers often get confused. A japa mala is strung on thread and meant to be moved bead by bead through the fingers. A rudraksha chain necklace usually sets fewer beads along a metal chain, often with a pendant such as Om, a trishul or Ganesha. It is made to be worn, not counted on.

Both have their place. If you want to chant 108 repetitions every morning, pick a thread mala with a guru bead. If you want something devotional to wear with daily clothes or on a festival day, a chain style is easier to put on, sits neatly at the neckline and pairs well with other jewellery. The [rudraksha chain necklaces at Varaha](/divine) are this second kind: fashion and devotional pieces with gold-plated pendants, not certified or graded beads.

sections.heading: Who can wear rudraksha?
paragraphs: Most traditions say rudraksha is open to everyone, irrespective of age or gender. Some families, though, follow their own rules: removing the mala before sleeping, during a period of mourning, or before eating non-vegetarian food. Others never take it off. Neither approach is wrong. They reflect different regional and family practices, and both are respected.

If you are unsure, the simplest path is to ask an elder at home or the priest at the temple your family visits. Their guidance will match the customs you already follow, which matters more than any general rule you read online.

sections.heading: A quick checklist before you buy
paragraphs: Whether you are buying for yourself or as a gift, these few checks save a lot of disappointment later.
list: Decide the purpose first: chanting (a thread mala of 108 plus one) or wearing (a chain or a shorter string).
Look at the bead surface. Rudraksha has irregular grooves and slight differences in size and colour from bead to bead.
Be wary of big promises. A seller guaranteeing a specific result from a bead is a red flag, not a selling point.
For chain styles, check the clasp and the pendant plating, since these take the most daily wear.
Think about length. Around 18 to 20 inches sits near the collarbone; longer lengths fall over a kurta.

faq.q: Can women wear a rudraksha mala?
faq.a: Yes. Most traditions say anyone can wear rudraksha. A few families follow their own restrictions, so it is worth checking the customs in your home.

faq.q: How many beads are in a rudraksha mala?
faq.a: A traditional japa mala has 108 beads plus one guru bead. Shorter malas of 54 or 27 beads, and wrist malas, are also common.

faq.q: Is it okay to wear rudraksha just for style?
faq.a: Many people do. If you wear one, treat it with basic respect, such as keeping it clean and taking it off where your tradition asks you to.
